problemStatement.formal:
Given some initial finite sequence of primes $q_1<\cdots<q_m$ extend it so that $q_{n+1}$ is the smallest prime of the form $q_n+q_i-1$ for $n\geq m$. Is there an initial starting sequence so that the resulting sequence is infinite?



A problem due to Ulam. For example if we begin with $3,5$ then the sequence continues $3,5,7,11,13,17,\ldots$. It is possible that this sequence is infinite.

insights: File is well-developed: 19 theorems including computational verification of 8 terms
Single axiom ulam35_contains_all_odd_primes_conjecture is genuinely open
The {3,5} Ulam sequence is conjectured to contain all odd primes
Computational step function (ulamNextCandidate, ulamStep, ulamExtend) enables native_decide verification
List.Sorted deprecated in current Mathlib in favor of List.Pairwise
seed_two_gives_even was incorrectly stated for all p >= 3 - only true for odd p
General structural bound: for seeds with all primes ≥ 3, strict monotonicity gives f(n) ≥ 3 for all n
Oddness preserved: since 2 is the only even prime and all terms are ≥ 3, all terms are odd — this means the parity argument in odd_candidate_from_odd applies to every step
Both seed elements 3 and 5 always appear in subsequent candidate lists — this is the key structural observation enabling exact stepping
Twin prime step: whenever f(n) and f(n)+2 are both prime, the sequence advances by exactly 2. This is the tightest possible step (gap bound says ≥ 2).
Cousin prime bound: f(n)+4 is always a candidate when prime (via 5 in seq), so f(n+1) ≤ f(n)+4 in that case. Combining: if either f(n)+2 or f(n)+4 is prime, f(n+1) ≤ f(n)+4.
The twin prime conjecture implies the {3,5} Ulam sequence contains infinitely many twin prime steps — but this is weaker than proving the sequence is infinite.
f(n)+3 is always composite in the {3,5} Ulam sequence: f(n) is odd → f(n)+3 = odd+odd = even, and even ≥ 6 is not prime.
Gap refinement: if f(n)+2 is not prime, then f(n+1) ≥ f(n)+4. Proof: f(n+1) ≠ f(n)+2 (not prime) and f(n+1) ≠ f(n)+3 (composite by parity).
Self-candidate bound: 2f(n)-1 is always a candidate (f(n) in its own list), so f(n+1) ≤ 2f(n)-1 when prime.
nextSteps: Prove: if f(n)+2 is NOT prime, then f(n+1) ≥ f(n)+4 (complement of twin prime step)
Formalize: f(n+1) = f(n)+4 when f(n)+2 composite and f(n)+4 prime (cousin prime exact step)
Upper bound from full sequence: f(n+1) ≤ f(n) + f(n) - 1 = 2f(n) - 1 when 2f(n)-1 is prime
